compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
All six examples use the same proposal materials, preparation time, supervisor feedback, deadline, and decision authority.

Each row compares two criteria either person can use for the same decision. The examples illustrate T/F as a difference in emphasis.

| Same proposal and decision | INFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing one of three viable topics | Which option best reflects the priorities of the people affected? | Which option meets the same criteria for clear definitions and sufficient evidence? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Evaluating the same research papers | How well does each study account for the circumstances of different participants? | Do comparable claims meet the same standard of evidence? | T/F: participants’ circumstances and consistent criteria. Both matter. |
| Narrowing the topic after the same feedback | Which revision keeps the question that matters to the people affected? | Which revision best meets the same requirements for scope and clarity? | T/F: relevance to people and consistently applied requirements |
| Deciding whether to use the same measure | Does it represent experiences that matter to the people being studied? | Would it meet the same measurement criteria when applied across comparable cases? | T/F: relevance to people and consistent standards for measurement |
| Framing the same evidence-based conclusion | How might the wording affect participants and readers? | Does the wording apply the same limits to comparable claims? | T/F: effects on people and consistent limits on claims |
| Choosing what to emphasize in the proposal defense | Which point makes clear why this question matters to those affected? | Which point shows how the proposal meets the same standard as comparable work? | T/F: purpose for people and consistency of the evaluation criteria |

Experience can shape which question someone is responsible for answering. Both people can check how the work affects participants and whether its claims meet the same standards. This table cannot measure research ability or identify a type.
compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In an early proposal meeting, either person might ask to see more evidence before settling on a topic. That can reflect the stage of the work as much as any preference.

Their shared I describes attention and energy directed more toward inner ideas and reflection. N emphasizes connections, patterns, and possibilities. P favors keeping options open in dealings with the outside world.

Deadline pressure, task difficulty, and habits can affect when someone starts writing or how often they revise. These behaviors cannot establish I, N, or P.

T/F concerns which criteria carry weight in a choice. Someone can ask whether a question matters to the people affected and whether all options meet the same standard of evidence. The two checks can guide the same decision.

### INFP and INTP: the same three-line outline, and how the two standards show up

In a fictional proposal review, two students have the same three-line outline, evidence, deadline, and authority to suggest changes. One question is which option best respects the priorities of the people affected. Another is which option meets the same standard for clear definitions and sufficient evidence.

An INFP can question a definition or check a citation. An INTP can ask how the proposed work would affect participants. These are skills anyone can develop, and either student can raise both concerns.

A compelling question still needs evidence that can answer it. A tightly defined question needs a reason to pursue it. Check both before revising the proposal.

The supervisor’s feedback, available records, and submission deadline may determine what gets revised first. That sequence cannot identify a type.

### INFP and INTP: what the stacks swap is the two judging ends

In type dynamics, the P in both codes points to an outward-facing perceiving process. Because both types are introverted, their outward process is auxiliary. Both show Ne in that position. The dominant judging process is inward-facing: Fi for INFP and Ti for INTP.

This page shows INFP as Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP as Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Ne is shared, and Si is shared under this notation. The first and fourth positions use different judging processes. The arrangement cannot tell you who reasons better or who acts first.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for both types, with Se or Si as alternatives. This page uses Si for both. The alternatives leave the dominant and auxiliary positions unchanged. See the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) and [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for more detail.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
All four examples are fictional. They show how people can weigh two kinds of criteria in the same situation. Speaking order and response speed cannot establish a preference.

When colleagues review the same proposal, ask which question each comment addresses and whether both concerns have been covered.

### INFP and INTP: two comments on the same draft proposal

In this fictional review, two students read the same draft. One comment asks whose concern the proposed question addresses. Another asks whether the draft treats the same concept consistently. Either student could offer both comments.

Record the comments separately. One identifies whose priorities need to be represented. The other identifies what needs defining and verifying. Compare the revisions to make sure the new definition still addresses the question.

Check that the draft says who the question matters to and what evidence would answer it. Both checks matter regardless of which one was raised first.

### INFP and INTP: the defence, and two ways to argue necessity

In this fictional proposal defense, both students receive the same question about why the project matters. Either can explain what the question means for the people affected and how the project meets the panel’s stated criteria.

A worked example can give the panel context. A clear account of the gap and proposed evidence can explain why the work is justified. Choose the emphasis from the actual question and the panel’s requirements.

Either student can prepare both answers. What they say in one defense can reflect practice and the questions asked.

### INFP and INTP: a hard methods course — drop it or not

In this fictional course decision, both students find the same methods course harder than expected. They have the same course description and proposal deadline. Compare what the course teaches, the prerequisites, the work required, and available alternatives.

Either student can weigh how much the method matters for a question they value and whether the course meets the same requirements they would apply to another option. The time available and actual project needs can decide the choice.

### INFP and INTP: an old friend sends a year's worth of writing

In this fictional example, a friend sends a manuscript they have worked on for a year. Either reviewer can ask what feedback would help, then consider what came through in the writing and where the argument was difficult to follow.

One paragraph can explain what the draft conveyed well. Another can point to a particular gap and suggest what the author might clarify. Either type can write both. Tailor the level of detail to what the author wants and the stage of the draft.

The author’s first reply may tell you what they want to discuss that day. Ask which feedback was useful if you need to know. Reply order does not reveal either person’s type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Neither having feelings nor challenging a claim can establish T/F. Both types can care deeply about a question and ask for better evidence.

Task difficulty, time pressure, and personal routine can affect when someone submits. One submission time cannot distinguish INFP from INTP.

A proposal is evaluated on its question, method, and reasoning. The criteria someone emphasizes do not measure rigor or concern for others.

One draft or reply can reflect the role, deadline, and information available. Treat a single example as context for a conversation, not a way to determine type.

**Fictional examples:** The proposal review, defense, course decision, and friend’s manuscript illustrate possible ways to weigh information. The framework sources do not establish how often either type behaves as shown.

**Scope limits**: scores and labels from different instruments should not be compared directly, and this page does not claim that either standard is more rigorous; results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships. compare_blocks.body:

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
All six examples use the same proposal materials, preparation time, supervisor feedback, deadline, and decision authority.

Each row compares two criteria either person can use for the same decision. The examples illustrate T/F as a difference in emphasis.

| Same proposal and decision | INFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing one of three viable topics | Which option best reflects the priorities of the people affected? | Which option meets the same criteria for clear definitions and sufficient evidence? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Evaluating the same research papers | How well does each study account for the circumstances of different participants? | Do comparable claims meet the same standard of evidence? | T/F: participants’ circumstances and consistent criteria. Both matter. |
| Narrowing the topic after the same feedback | Which revision keeps the question that matters to the people affected? | Which revision best meets the same requirements for scope and clarity? | T/F: relevance to people and consistently applied requirements |
| Deciding whether to use the same measure | Does it represent experiences that matter to the people being studied? | Would it meet the same measurement criteria when applied across comparable cases? | T/F: relevance to people and consistent standards for measurement |
| Framing the same evidence-based conclusion | How might the wording affect participants and readers? | Does the wording apply the same limits to comparable claims? | T/F: effects on people and consistent limits on claims |
| Choosing what to emphasize in the proposal defense | Which point makes clear why this question matters to those affected? | Which point shows how the proposal meets the same standard as comparable work? | T/F: purpose for people and consistency of the evaluation criteria |

Experience can shape which question someone is responsible for answering. Both people can check how the work affects participants and whether its claims meet the same standards. This table cannot measure research ability or identify a type.
compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In an early proposal meeting, either person might ask to see more evidence before settling on a topic. That can reflect the stage of the work as much as any preference.

Their shared I describes attention and energy directed more toward inner ideas and reflection. N emphasizes connections, patterns, and possibilities. P favors keeping options open in dealings with the outside world.

Deadline pressure, task difficulty, and habits can affect when someone starts writing or how often they revise. These behaviors cannot establish I, N, or P.

T/F concerns which criteria carry weight in a choice. Someone can ask whether a question matters to the people affected and whether all options meet the same standard of evidence. The two checks can guide the same decision.

### INFP and INTP: the same three-line outline, and how the two standards show up

In a fictional proposal review, two students have the same three-line outline, evidence, deadline, and authority to suggest changes. One question is which option best respects the priorities of the people affected. Another is which option meets the same standard for clear definitions and sufficient evidence.

An INFP can question a definition or check a citation. An INTP can ask how the proposed work would affect participants. These are skills anyone can develop, and either student can raise both concerns.

A compelling question still needs evidence that can answer it. A tightly defined question needs a reason to pursue it. Check both before revising the proposal.

The supervisor’s feedback, available records, and submission deadline may determine what gets revised first. That sequence cannot identify a type.

### INFP and INTP: what the stacks swap is the two judging ends

In type dynamics, the P in both codes points to an outward-facing perceiving process. Because both types are introverted, their outward process is auxiliary. Both show Ne in that position. The dominant judging process is inward-facing: Fi for INFP and Ti for INTP.

This page shows INFP as Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP as Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Ne is shared, and Si is shared under this notation. The first and fourth positions use different judging processes. The arrangement cannot tell you who reasons better or who acts first.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for both types, with Se or Si as alternatives. This page uses Si for both. The alternatives leave the dominant and auxiliary positions unchanged. See the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) and [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for more detail.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
All four examples are fictional. They show how people can weigh two kinds of criteria in the same situation. Speaking order and response speed cannot establish a preference.

When colleagues review the same proposal, ask which question each comment addresses and whether both concerns have been covered.

### INFP and INTP: two comments on the same draft proposal

In this fictional review, two students read the same draft. One comment asks whose concern the proposed question addresses. Another asks whether the draft treats the same concept consistently. Either student could offer both comments.

Record the comments separately. One identifies whose priorities need to be represented. The other identifies what needs defining and verifying. Compare the revisions to make sure the new definition still addresses the question.

Check that the draft says who the question matters to and what evidence would answer it. Both checks matter regardless of which one was raised first.

### INFP and INTP: the defence, and two ways to argue necessity

In this fictional proposal defense, both students receive the same question about why the project matters. Either can explain what the question means for the people affected and how the project meets the panel’s stated criteria.

A worked example can give the panel context. A clear account of the gap and proposed evidence can explain why the work is justified. Choose the emphasis from the actual question and the panel’s requirements.

Either student can prepare both answers. What they say in one defense can reflect practice and the questions asked.

### INFP and INTP: a hard methods course — drop it or not

In this fictional course decision, both students find the same methods course harder than expected. They have the same course description and proposal deadline. Compare what the course teaches, the prerequisites, the work required, and available alternatives.

Either student can weigh how much the method matters for a question they value and whether the course meets the same requirements they would apply to another option. The time available and actual project needs can decide the choice.

### INFP and INTP: an old friend sends a year's worth of writing

In this fictional example, a friend sends a manuscript they have worked on for a year. Either reviewer can ask what feedback would help, then consider what came through in the writing and where the argument was difficult to follow.

One paragraph can explain what the draft conveyed well. Another can point to a particular gap and suggest what the author might clarify. Either type can write both. Tailor the level of detail to what the author wants and the stage of the draft.

The author’s first reply may tell you what they want to discuss that day. Ask which feedback was useful if you need to know. Reply order does not reveal either person’s type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Neither having feelings nor challenging a claim can establish T/F. Both types can care deeply about a question and ask for better evidence.

Task difficulty, time pressure, and personal routine can affect when someone submits. One submission time cannot distinguish INFP from INTP.

A proposal is evaluated on its question, method, and reasoning. The criteria someone emphasizes do not measure rigor or concern for others.

One draft or reply can reflect the role, deadline, and information available. Treat a single example as context for a conversation, not a way to determine type.

faq_blocks.answer:
INFP and INTP share Introversion, Intuition, and Perceiving. The only letter difference is T/F, which concerns which criteria carry weight in a decision.

An INFP and an INTP can both notice a weak argument or an overlooked consequence. Look at the reasons people give across comparable choices. Writing speed and edit order cannot establish a preference.
faq_blocks.question: Where are INFP and INTP most easily confused?

faq_blocks.answer:
In this notation, INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Fi and Ti are the respective dominant judging processes, supported by shared auxiliary Ne.

Both also show Si in the tertiary position in this convention. The Foundation gives Se or Si as alternatives. The inferior positions differ: Te for INFP and Fe for INTP. These positions do not establish ability or action order.
faq_blocks.question: Where do the two stacks differ?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. Either type can pursue a question that matters to them and check an argument for logical gaps.

For reflection, compare decisions where you had similar responsibilities and room to choose. Consider what evidence, values, and effects on people mattered. A single concern cannot establish T/F.
faq_blocks.question: INTP also holds to something on meaning, INFP also picks at logical gaps?

faq_blocks.answer:
Either type can do postgraduate research. Assess the topic, relevant training, supervision, and the actual work involved.

Try reviewing a proposal: explain whom the question matters to, what evidence would support an answer, and what is still missing. This gives you a clearer picture of the work without using type to allocate tasks.
faq_blocks.question: Which of the two is better suited to postgraduate research?

faq_blocks.answer:
A disagreement can arise when one comment addresses why a question matters and the other addresses the evidence that could answer it. Either person can raise either concern.

Write down the purpose, definitions, and limits on the claim. Assign the review by familiarity with the evidence and what the next reader needs. Then compare the revisions for consistency.
faq_blocks.question: Where does collaboration most often jam?

faq_blocks.answer:
Start with the instrument, version, language, and scoring guidance. Then consider what role or situation you had in mind when answering.

If comparable reports provide interpretable T/F scores, use the instrument’s guidance to interpret any score near its cutoff. A change in labels alone does not identify the cause.

jsonld.description: INFP and INTP share I, N, and P and differ only on Thinking vs. Feeling. Compare dominant Fi and Ti and see six examples of how they weigh the same decision.
jsonld.name: INFP vs INTP: Thinking, Feeling, and Cognitive Functions

sections.body_md:
INFP and INTP share Introversion, Intuition, and Perceiving. Their only letter difference is Feeling (F) for INFP and Thinking (T) for INTP.

Feeling emphasizes values and effects on people when making a decision. Thinking emphasizes principles, logical consistency, and criteria that can be applied consistently. Either type can consider both.

In the notation used here, INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. INFP leads with introverted Feeling (Fi), while INTP leads with introverted Thinking (Ti). Both share auxiliary extraverted Intuition (Ne). The Foundation gives alternatives for the attitude of their tertiary Sensing process.

Either type can improve an argument and ask why it matters to the people involved. The order of edits can reflect responsibilities, experience, or a deadline. It cannot distinguish T from F.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In an early proposal meeting, either person might ask to see more evidence before settling on a topic. That can reflect the stage of the work as much as any preference.

Their shared I describes attention and energy directed more toward inner ideas and reflection. N emphasizes connections, patterns, and possibilities. P favors keeping options open in dealings with the outside world.

Deadline pressure, task difficulty, and habits can affect when someone starts writing or how often they revise. These behaviors cannot establish I, N, or P.

T/F concerns which criteria carry weight in a choice. Someone can ask whether a question matters to the people affected and whether all options meet the same standard of evidence. The two checks can guide the same decision.

### INFP and INTP: the same three-line outline, and how the two standards show up

In a fictional proposal review, two students have the same three-line outline, evidence, deadline, and authority to suggest changes. One question is which option best respects the priorities of the people affected. Another is which option meets the same standard for clear definitions and sufficient evidence.

An INFP can question a definition or check a citation. An INTP can ask how the proposed work would affect participants. These are skills anyone can develop, and either student can raise both concerns.

A compelling question still needs evidence that can answer it. A tightly defined question needs a reason to pursue it. Check both before revising the proposal.

The supervisor’s feedback, available records, and submission deadline may determine what gets revised first. That sequence cannot identify a type.

### INFP and INTP: what the stacks swap is the two judging ends

In type dynamics, the P in both codes points to an outward-facing perceiving process. Because both types are introverted, their outward process is auxiliary. Both show Ne in that position. The dominant judging process is inward-facing: Fi for INFP and Ti for INTP.

This page shows INFP as Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP as Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Ne is shared, and Si is shared under this notation. The first and fourth positions use different judging processes. The arrangement cannot tell you who reasons better or who acts first.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for both types, with Se or Si as alternatives. This page uses Si for both. The alternatives leave the dominant and auxiliary positions unchanged. See the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) and [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for more detail.
sections.title: INFP and INTP: what they share, and where the one axis differs

sections.body_md:
All six examples use the same proposal materials, preparation time, supervisor feedback, deadline, and decision authority.

Each row compares two criteria either person can use for the same decision. The examples illustrate T/F as a difference in emphasis.

| Same proposal and decision | INFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing one of three viable topics | Which option best reflects the priorities of the people affected? | Which option meets the same criteria for clear definitions and sufficient evidence? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Evaluating the same research papers | How well does each study account for the circumstances of different participants? | Do comparable claims meet the same standard of evidence? | T/F: participants’ circumstances and consistent criteria. Both matter. |
| Narrowing the topic after the same feedback | Which revision keeps the question that matters to the people affected? | Which revision best meets the same requirements for scope and clarity? | T/F: relevance to people and consistently applied requirements |
| Deciding whether to use the same measure | Does it represent experiences that matter to the people being studied? | Would it meet the same measurement criteria when applied across comparable cases? | T/F: relevance to people and consistent standards for measurement |
| Framing the same evidence-based conclusion | How might the wording affect participants and readers? | Does the wording apply the same limits to comparable claims? | T/F: effects on people and consistent limits on claims |
| Choosing what to emphasize in the proposal defense | Which point makes clear why this question matters to those affected? | Which point shows how the proposal meets the same standard as comparable work? | T/F: purpose for people and consistency of the evaluation criteria |

Experience can shape which question someone is responsible for answering. Both people can check how the work affects participants and whether its claims meet the same standards. This table cannot measure research ability or identify a type.
sections.title: INFP and INTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
All four examples are fictional. They show how people can weigh two kinds of criteria in the same situation. Speaking order and response speed cannot establish a preference.

When colleagues review the same proposal, ask which question each comment addresses and whether both concerns have been covered.

### INFP and INTP: two comments on the same draft proposal

In this fictional review, two students read the same draft. One comment asks whose concern the proposed question addresses. Another asks whether the draft treats the same concept consistently. Either student could offer both comments.

Record the comments separately. One identifies whose priorities need to be represented. The other identifies what needs defining and verifying. Compare the revisions to make sure the new definition still addresses the question.

Check that the draft says who the question matters to and what evidence would answer it. Both checks matter regardless of which one was raised first.

### INFP and INTP: the defence, and two ways to argue necessity

In this fictional proposal defense, both students receive the same question about why the project matters. Either can explain what the question means for the people affected and how the project meets the panel’s stated criteria.

A worked example can give the panel context. A clear account of the gap and proposed evidence can explain why the work is justified. Choose the emphasis from the actual question and the panel’s requirements.

Either student can prepare both answers. What they say in one defense can reflect practice and the questions asked.

### INFP and INTP: a hard methods course — drop it or not

In this fictional course decision, both students find the same methods course harder than expected. They have the same course description and proposal deadline. Compare what the course teaches, the prerequisites, the work required, and available alternatives.

Either student can weigh how much the method matters for a question they value and whether the course meets the same requirements they would apply to another option. The time available and actual project needs can decide the choice.

### INFP and INTP: an old friend sends a year's worth of writing

In this fictional example, a friend sends a manuscript they have worked on for a year. Either reviewer can ask what feedback would help, then consider what came through in the writing and where the argument was difficult to follow.

One paragraph can explain what the draft conveyed well. Another can point to a particular gap and suggest what the author might clarify. Either type can write both. Tailor the level of detail to what the author wants and the stage of the draft.

The author’s first reply may tell you what they want to discuss that day. Ask which feedback was useful if you need to know. Reply order does not reveal either person’s type.
sections.title: INFP and INTP in four fictional scenarios

sections.body_md:
Neither having feelings nor challenging a claim can establish T/F. Both types can care deeply about a question and ask for better evidence.

Task difficulty, time pressure, and personal routine can affect when someone submits. One submission time cannot distinguish INFP from INTP.

A proposal is evaluated on its question, method, and reasoning. The criteria someone emphasizes do not measure rigor or concern for others.

One draft or reply can reflect the role, deadline, and information available. Treat a single example as context for a conversation, not a way to determine type.
sections.title: INFP and INTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
Compare the assessment, version, language, and scoring guidance. Think about which situations you had in mind when answering. Different instruments can use the same type labels without producing directly comparable scores.

If comparable reports give interpretable T/F scores, use the instrument’s guidance for scores near the cutoff. Different labels alone cannot show how close either score was or why a result changed.

Recall a decision where you had a real choice. Record which criteria applied equally to the options, who was affected, and what mattered to them. Ask what new evidence or change in circumstances would alter your decision.

Use the notes for reflection and include examples where your emphasis changed. They do not produce a score or determine a type.
sections.title: INFP and INTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
INFP and INTP share Introversion, Intuition, and Perceiving. The only letter difference is T/F, which concerns which criteria carry weight in a decision.

An INFP and an INTP can both notice a weak argument or an overlooked consequence. Look at the reasons people give across comparable choices. Writing speed and edit order cannot establish a preference.
items.question: Where are INFP and INTP most easily confused?

items.answer:
In this notation, INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Fi and Ti are the respective dominant judging processes, supported by shared auxiliary Ne.

Both also show Si in the tertiary position in this convention. The Foundation gives Se or Si as alternatives. The inferior positions differ: Te for INFP and Fe for INTP. These positions do not establish ability or action order.
items.question: Where do the two stacks differ?

items.answer:
Yes. Either type can pursue a question that matters to them and check an argument for logical gaps.

For reflection, compare decisions where you had similar responsibilities and room to choose. Consider what evidence, values, and effects on people mattered. A single concern cannot establish T/F.
items.question: INTP also holds to something on meaning, INFP also picks at logical gaps?

items.answer:
Either type can do postgraduate research. Assess the topic, relevant training, supervision, and the actual work involved.

Try reviewing a proposal: explain whom the question matters to, what evidence would support an answer, and what is still missing. This gives you a clearer picture of the work without using type to allocate tasks.
items.question: Which of the two is better suited to postgraduate research?

items.answer:
A disagreement can arise when one comment addresses why a question matters and the other addresses the evidence that could answer it. Either person can raise either concern.

Write down the purpose, definitions, and limits on the claim. Assign the review by familiarity with the evidence and what the next reader needs. Then compare the revisions for consistency.
items.question: Where does collaboration most often jam?

items.answer:
Start with the instrument, version, language, and scoring guidance. Then consider what role or situation you had in mind when answering.

If comparable reports provide interpretable T/F scores, use the instrument’s guidance to interpret any score near its cutoff. A change in labels alone does not identify the cause.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources**: the definitions of the preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function notation:** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te for INFP and Ti–Ne–Si–Fe for INTP. The Foundation gives alternatives for the tertiary attitude. The first two positions stay the same.

**Fictional examples:** The proposal review, defense, course decision, and friend’s manuscript illustrate possible ways to weigh information. The framework sources do not establish how often either type behaves as shown.

**Scope limits**: scores and labels from different instruments should not be compared directly, and this page does not claim that either standard is more rigorous; results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships. The FermatMind assessment uses a separate item bank and scoring; its scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
